messages.content: What is the acceleration a ball will reach if it's thrown straight upwards with a velocity of 5 m/s?

function.name: calculate_maximum_height
function.description: Calculate the maximum height an object will reach if it's thrown straight upwards with an initial velocity, ignoring air resistance. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

initial_velocity.description: The initial velocity in meters per second. This is a float type value.

gravity.description: The acceleration due to gravity in meters per second squared, default value is 9.8. This is a float type value.

message.content:
When you throw a ball upward, it’s still subject to Earth’s gravity pulling it back downwards.  
Gravity provides a **constant** acceleration of roughly \(g \approx 9.8\;\text{m/s}^{2}\) directed toward the ground—so we usually write this as \(-9.8\;\text{m/s}^{2}\) when using a coordinate system where “up” is positive.

So no matter what your launch speed is (e.g., \(v_0=5\,\text{m/s}\)), the ball’s instantaneous acceleration while moving up or falling back down stays:

\[
a = -9.8\;\text{m/s}^{2}
\]

(If you’re working in SI units and neglecting air resistance.)
message.reasoning:
The user asks "What is the acceleration a ball will reach if it's thrown straight upwards with a velocity of 5 m/s?" They likely want gravitational acceleration downward (i.e., -9.81). But they might misunderstand; maybe they think about acceleration at top where velocity zero? Actually acceleration remains constant g regardless of speed. So answer: approximately -9.8 m/s^2.
